title: Πρωτέως Μαντεία καὶ Νοήμονος Ἀγγελία
titleEn: Proteus's Prophecy and Noemon's News — Odyssey 4.538–640
about: Proteus, mastered by Menelaus, ends his long account of the Achaean captains' returns: he consoles Menelaus, promises he will not die but pass to the Elysian plain, and reveals that Odysseus alone still lives, held against his will by the nymph Calypso. Proteus sinks beneath the sea, and Menelaus completes his own tale to Telemachus — the voyage back to Egypt, the sacrifices, Agamemnon's tomb, and the calm return home. Menelaus urges Telemachus to stay longer, but Telemachus, homesick for rocky Ithaca, asks to leave with only a keepsake, and Menelaus gives him a wrought silver bowl once given by the king of Sidon. The scene shifts to Ithaca, where the suitors are at their games; Noemon asks Antinous for his ship back and lets slip that Telemachus has sailed to Pylos — news that leaves the suitors amazed, since they had thought him still at home among the flocks.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γε κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ,
κλαῖον δ’ ἐν ψαμάθοισι καθήμενος, οὐδέ νύ μοι κῆρ
ἤθελ’ ἔτι ζώειν καὶ ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and my own heart was broken within me,
and I wept, sitting among the sands, nor at all did my heart
wish still to live and to look upon the light of the sun.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and my heart was broken within me: I sat weeping among the sands, and I no longer wished to go on living and to see the light of the sun.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ(ο), 'so he spoke', is the narrator's tag that closes Proteus's long third speech, begun at 4.492 in the previous part and left there without a closing mark because its content, Agamemnon's murder and its aftermath, continued past that part's boundary; its actual last words were 4.537. κατεκλάσθη, an aorist passive of κατακλάω 'break down, shatter', repeats 4.481 word for word, a purely formulaic recurrence for a different grief. κῆρ is a poetic word for 'heart', distinct from κραδίη and ἦτορ, both used nearby.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κλαίων τε κυλινδόμενός τε κορέσθην,
δὴ τότε με προσέειπε γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής·
sentences.l:
But when of weeping and of rolling-about I had my fill,
then indeed addressed me the unerring old man of the sea:
sentences.i: But when I had had enough of weeping and writhing on the ground, then the unerring old man of the sea spoke to me:
sentences.n: κορέσθην is an aorist passive-in-form (deponent) of κορέννυμι 'sate, glut'; rather than the genitive noun this verb usually takes for the thing one has had enough of, here it takes two nominative participles, κλαίων and κυλινδόμενος, 'weeping' and 'rolling about (in grief)', agreeing with the subject in the ordinary Homeric supplementary-participle construction (as with verbs of ceasing). γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής is Proteus's already-fixed standing epithet. This line introduces Proteus's fourth speech in the part, distinct from the long third speech just closed; the mark and opening quotation belong to the next unit.

sentences.t:
μηκέτι, Ἀτρέος υἱέ, πολὺν χρόνον ἀσκελὲς οὕτω
κλαῖ’, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἄνυσίν τινα δήομεν·
sentences.l:
“No longer, son of Atreus, for a long time, unyieldingly, thus
weep, since no accomplishment at all shall we find;
sentences.i: “Weep no longer, son of Atreus, so long and so unyieldingly, since we shall find no help in it;
sentences.n: μηκέτι with the imperative κλαῖε (elided κλαῖ’) is a prohibition, 'stop weeping'; the imperative is delayed to the start of 544 while its modifiers pile up first. ἀσκελές, 'stubbornly, unyieldingly', was used of Poseidon's anger at 1.68; here it describes Menelaus's grief instead. ἄνυσις, 'accomplishment, result' (from ἀνύω), and δήομεν, a short-vowel aorist subjunctive of a defective verb 'find' (= δαήσομεν), give a near-future sense, 'we shall find'. This opens Proteus's fourth speech, so it takes a fresh opening quotation mark.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τάχιστα
πείρα ὅπως κεν δὴ σὴν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκηαι.
sentences.l:
but with all speed
try how you may indeed reach your own fatherland.
sentences.i: but try with all speed to find a way to reach your own native land.
sentences.n: πείρα is a present imperative of πειράω 'try, attempt' (distinct from πείρω 'pierce'; context and accent show the imperative here). ὅπως κεν with the subjunctive ἵκηαι, 'how you may come', gives the object of the trying; κεν is the epic equivalent of ἄν. σὴν πατρίδα γαῖαν, 'your own fatherland', pairs the possessive adjective with γαῖα as at 1.41 (ἣν γαῖαν).

sentences.t:
ἢ γάρ μιν ζωόν γε κιχήσεαι, ἤ κεν Ὀρέστης
κτεῖνεν ὑποφθάμενος, σὺ δέ κεν τάφου ἀντιβολήσαις.
sentences.l:
For either you shall come upon him yet alive,
or Orestes will have killed him, forestalling; and you might come upon his funeral.”
sentences.i: for either you will find him still alive, or Orestes will already have forestalled you and killed him, and you may come in time for his funeral.”
sentences.n: μιν and the understood object of κτεῖνεν are both Aegisthus, left unnamed here because he has just been named at length in the preceding speech (4.524–537, previous part). κτεῖνεν is an aorist indicative used with future force, a Homeric idiom for an act pictured as already accomplished by the time it matters. ὑποφθάμενος is the aorist participle of ὑποφθάνω 'get ahead of, forestall'. τάφου, genitive with ἀντιβολήσαις (optative of ἀντιβολέω 'meet, come upon' + genitive), is 'the funeral rites'. This closes Proteus's fourth speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
αὖτις ἐνὶ στήθεσσι καὶ ἀχνυμένῳ περ ἰάνθη,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and my heart and my manly spirit
again within my breast, grieved though I was, were warmed,
and speaking to him, winged words I addressed to him:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and my heart and my proud spirit were warmed again within my breast, grieved though I still was, and I spoke to him and addressed him with winged words:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ(ο) again closes the speech just given. κραδίη and θυμός, both words for the seat of feeling, are paired for emphasis, as ἦτορ and κῆρ were at 4.538 and 4.539. ἀγήνωρ, 'manly, proud-spirited', is a common Homeric epithet of θυμός, fixed here as 'manly spirit' — see new-renderings.md. ἰάνθη is an aorist passive of ἰαίνω 'warm, gladden'. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων is the already-fixed 'winged words' formula, here imperfect first person rather than the usual aorist, since Menelaus is narrating.

sentences.t: τούτους μὲν δὴ οἶδα·
sentences.l: ‘These men, then, indeed I know;
sentences.i: ‘These men, then, I know well;
sentences.n: τούτους refers back to Ajax and Agamemnon, whose fates Proteus has just related; μέν δή is emphatic, 'these, at any rate'. This opens Menelaus's own recalled speech to Proteus, nested inside his still-open outer narration to Telemachus (begun at 4.333); per the scheme already fixed in odyssey-018, his own recalled words take a single ‘ ’ pair rather than a fresh “ ”.
sentences.mark: Menelaus recalls his third question to Proteus

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ τρίτον ἄνδρ’ ὀνόμαζε,
ὅς τις ἔτι ζωὸς κατερύκεται εὐρέι πόντῳ
ἠὲ θανών·
sentences.i: but tell me the name of a third man — whether he is still alive, held somewhere on the broad sea, or has died;
sentences.n: ὀνόμαζε is a present imperative, 'name, tell the name of'; the 'third man' is Odysseus, though Menelaus does not yet know it. κατερύκεται, present passive, 'is held back, detained', anticipates the same idea in the different verb Proteus will use of Calypso's hold on him (ἴσχει, 558). εὐρέι πόντῳ is a plain descriptive dative, 'on the broad sea', distinct from the already-fixed epithet ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο.

sentences.t: ἐθέλω δὲ καὶ ἀχνύμενός περ ἀκοῦσαι.
sentences.l: and I wish, grieved though I am, to hear it.’
sentences.i: I want to hear, however painful it may be.’
sentences.n: ἀχνύμενός περ, 'grieved though I am', is the same concessive περ-with-participle construction seen throughout the poem (cf. 1.6, ἱέμενός περ); ἀκοῦσαι is the aorist infinitive object of ἐθέλω. This closes Menelaus's recalled question to Proteus.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:
sentences.i: So I said, and he answered me at once:
sentences.n: This whole line is identical to 4.471 and 4.491, both already published in odyssey-018, where this reply-formula was first fixed as a new house rendering; the identical English is required here too, since the Greek is byte-for-byte the same.

sentences.t: υἱὸς Λαέρτεω, Ἰθάκῃ ἔνι οἰκία ναίων·
sentences.l: “The son of Laertes, in Ithaca dwelling in a house;
sentences.i: “It is the son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca;
sentences.n: The sentence has no expressed verb 'is': Proteus answers with a bare identification, the patronymic υἱὸς Λαέρτεω, 'son of Laertes', standing for the name Ὀδυσσεύς, never spoken in this speech. ναίων, present participle of ναίω 'dwell', agrees with an understood 'he'. This opens Proteus's fifth and final speech in the part, a fresh top-level quotation, since the intervening narration (548–554) has closed the fourth.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἴδον ἐν νήσῳ θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντα,
νύμφης ἐν μεγάροισι Καλυψοῦς, ἥ μιν ἀνάγκῃ
ἴσχει·
sentences.i: but I saw him on an island, shedding a swelling tear, in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him there against his will;
sentences.n: κατὰ ... χέοντα is tmesis for καταχέοντα, 'pouring down'; θαλερὸν... δάκρυ, 'a swelling tear' (θαλερός 'blooming, vigorous', here of copious tears), varies the already-fixed δάκρυ χέων 'a tear shedding' with an added adjective, kept literal. ἀνάγκῃ is a dative of manner, 'by constraint, of necessity'. ἴσχει, 'holds, restrains', anticipates κατερύκεται at 552 in reverse. Calypso is named here for the first time in Menelaus's own account.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ οὐ δύναται ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι·
sentences.l: but he is not able his own fatherland to reach;
sentences.i: and he cannot reach his own native land;
sentences.n: ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν, 'his own fatherland', repeats the possessive ὅς-adjective already met at 1.41 and 4.475; δύναται is present, matching ἴσχει just before. This states plainly, well before Menelaus can have any inkling, exactly the situation the poem's audience has already been shown in Book 1.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ οἱ πάρα νῆες ἐπήρετμοι καὶ ἑταῖροι,
οἵ κέν μιν πέμποιεν ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
For he has no oared ships nor companions,
who might send him over the broad back of the sea.
sentences.i: for he has no oared ships or companions who might convey him over the sea's broad back.
sentences.n: πάρα is πάρεστι, 'are at hand', with the accent thrown back as in anastrophe; ἐπήρετμοι, 'fitted with oars', is a compound of ἐπί and ἐρετμόν. πέμποιεν is a potential optative in a relative clause of characteristic. ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης is the already-fixed formula (cf. 3.362), 'the broad back of the sea'.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ οὐ θέσφατόν ἐστι, διοτρεφὲς ὦ Μενέλαε,
Ἄργει ἐν ἱπποβότῳ θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν,
ἀλλά σ’ ἐς Ἠλύσιον πεδίον καὶ πείρατα γαίης
ἀθάνατοι πέμψουσιν, ὅθι ξανθὸς Ῥαδάμανθυς,
τῇ περ ῥηίστη βιοτὴ πέλει ἀνθρώποισιν·
sentences.l:
But for you it is not god-declared, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus,
in horse-pasturing Argos to die and to meet your fate,
but to the Elysian plain and the ends of the earth
the immortals will send you, where fair-haired Rhadamanthus is,
where indeed the easiest life there is for men;
sentences.i: But it is not decreed for you, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, to die in horse-pasturing Argos and meet your fate there; instead the immortal gods will send you to the Elysian plain, at the ends of the earth, where fair-haired Rhadamanthus dwells, and where life is easiest for men;
sentences.n: θέσφατόν ἐστι, 'it is declared by a god, fated' (θεός + φημί), is a new formula fixed here — see new-renderings.md. διοτρεφές is the already-fixed 'Zeus-nurtured'. ἱπποβότῳ, 'horse-pasturing', describes Argos proper. Ἠλύσιον πεδίον, 'the Elysian plain', is a paradise at the world's edge for a few favoured mortals, spared ordinary death; ξανθός, 'fair-haired', is the same epithet already fixed for Menelaus himself, now applied to Rhadamanthus. ὅθι and τῇ περ, both 'where', are doubled relatives in apposition, a common Homeric emphasis; ῥηίστη is the superlative of ῥᾴδιος 'easy'.

sentences.t:
οὐ νιφετός, οὔτ’ ἂρ χειμὼν πολὺς οὔτε ποτ’ ὄμβρος,
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ Ζεφύροιο λιγὺ πνείοντος ἀήτας
Ὠκεανὸς ἀνίησιν ἀναψύχειν ἀνθρώπους·
sentences.i: there is no snow, nor much storm, nor ever rain, but Oceanus always sends up the shrill-blowing breezes of the West Wind to refresh mankind;
sentences.n: νιφετός 'snowfall', χειμών 'winter storm' and ὄμβρος 'rain-storm' are the hardships Elysium lacks. Ζεφύροιο λιγὺ πνείοντος, 'of the West Wind blowing shrill', is a genitive phrase modifying ἀήτας, 'gusts, breezes', which is itself the accusative object of ἀνίησιν. Oceanus, the great river encircling the world, is pictured sending up these breezes at its outer edge; ἀναψύχειν is an epexegetic infinitive, 'so as to refresh'.

sentences.t: οὕνεκ’ ἔχεις Ἑλένην καί σφιν γαμβρὸς Διός ἐσσι.
sentences.l: because you have Helen, and to them you are the son-in-law of Zeus.”
sentences.i: because you have Helen for your wife, and are son-in-law to Zeus.”
sentences.n: οὕνεκα, 'because', gives the reason for Menelaus's exemption from ordinary death: his marriage to Helen. σφιν, 'to them', refers to the gods collectively, the ἀθάνατοι of 564. γαμβρός, 'son-in-law, relative by marriage'; since Helen is a daughter of Zeus (cf. 4.184), Menelaus counts as his kinsman. This closes Proteus's fifth speech, the last he is given in this part.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὑπὸ πόντον ἐδύσετο κυμαίνοντα.
sentences.l: So speaking, beneath the surging sea he sank down.
sentences.i: So speaking, he sank down beneath the surging sea.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών, 'so speaking', is Proteus's own exit-formula, grammatically distinct from the narrator's speech-closing ὣς ἔφατ(ο): it is a participle agreeing with the subject of ἐδύσετο (aorist of δύω 'sink, dive') rather than an independent clause. κυμαίνοντα, 'surging, billowing' (from κῦμα 'wave'), describes the sea as Proteus disappears into it, the last the poem shows of him.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπὶ νῆας ἅμ’ ἀντιθέοις ἑτάροισιν
ἤια, πολλὰ δέ μοι κραδίη πόρφυρε κιόντι.
sentences.l:
But I to the ships together with my godlike companions
went, and much did my heart darkly-brood as I went.
sentences.i: But I went back to the ships with my godlike companions, my heart darkly troubled the whole way.
sentences.n: ἤια is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go'. ἀντίθεος, 'godlike', is the already-fixed general epithet for companions. πόρφυρε, imperfect of πορφύρω, literally 'grow dark, seethe' (of a swelling sea), used metaphorically of a mind churning over many thoughts, the same image behind English 'brooding'; κιόντι, present participle of an old verb 'go', agrees with the dative μοι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλθομεν ἠδὲ θάλασσαν,
δόρπον θ’ ὁπλισάμεσθ’, ἐπί τ’ ἤλυθεν ἀμβροσίη νύξ,
δὴ τότε κοιμήθημεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
But when then we had come down to the ship and the sea,
we made ready our supper, and upon it came ambrosial night,
then indeed we lay down to sleep upon the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: But when we had come down to the ship and the sea and got supper ready, and ambrosial night came on, then we lay down to sleep on the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: κατήλθομεν, 'we came down' (from κατέρχομαι), is a different aorist stem from the κατήλυθον already shipped at the parallel line 4.428 (odyssey-017); the two forms are synonyms, and the difference is metrical, not one of sense. The second and third lines are otherwise identical, word for word, to lines already published at 4.429 and 4.430 (odyssey-017), and their English is repeated here, adapted only in trailing punctuation to fit this sentence's own continuation and close.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
νῆας μὲν πάμπρωτον ἐρύσσαμεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν,
ἐν δ’ ἱστοὺς τιθέμεσθα καὶ ἱστία νηυσὶν ἐίσῃς,
ἂν δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ βάντες ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον·
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
first of all we drew the ships down into the heavenly brine,
and we set in them the masts, and the sails, in the well-balanced ships,
and we ourselves too, having gone aboard, upon the rowing-benches were sitting down;
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, first of all we drew the ships down into the bright sea, stepped the masts and sails in the well-balanced ships, and climbed aboard ourselves and sat down at the oarlocks;
sentences.n: ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς is the already-fixed whole-line dawn-formula. ἅλα δῖαν, 'the heavenly brine', keeps the table's rendering of δῖος 'heavenly' even applied to the sea (compare the noted inconsistency at this same phrase, ἅλα δῖαν, 3.153, flagged in the conventions table under the Λακεδαίμων δῖα row, where the i-layer instead used 'bright'). νηυσὶν ἐίσῃς is the already-fixed 'well-balanced ships'. The line's second half is word for word identical to a line already published at 4.418 (odyssey-008), and its English is reused, though its own preceding line there differed from ours.

sentences.t: ἑξῆς δ’ ἑζόμενοι πολιὴν ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.l: and sitting in a row, the grey sea they struck with their oars.
sentences.i: and sitting in rows, they struck the grey sea with their oars.
sentences.n: ἑξῆς, 'in a row, in order', is the same adverb already used of the seals at 4.440 and 448 (odyssey-018). πολιὴν ἅλα is the already-fixed 'the grey sea'. τύπτον, imperfect of τύπτω 'strike, beat', pictures the steady rhythm of rowing.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ εἰς Αἰγύπτοιο διιπετέος ποταμοῖο
στῆσα νέας, καὶ ἔρεξα τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας.
sentences.l:
And back to Egypt's sky-fallen river
I brought the ships to rest, and I offered complete hecatombs.
sentences.i: And I brought the ships back to the river of Egypt, fallen from the sky, and there I offered complete hecatombs.
sentences.n: ἂψ, 'back again', marks the return voyage Proteus had prescribed at 4.477–478 (odyssey-018). διιπετέος, 'fallen from the sky' (Διός + πίπτω), is the already-fixed epithet of the Nile. στῆσα, aorist of ἵστημι, is transitive, 'brought to a stand, moored'. τεληέσσας, 'complete, unblemished' (from τέλος), is a stock epithet of a proper sacrifice, fixed here as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατέπαυσα θεῶν χόλον αἰὲν ἐόντων,
χεῦ’ Ἀγαμέμνονι τύμβον, ἵν’ ἄσβεστον κλέος εἴη.
sentences.l:
But when I had stayed the anger of the gods who are forever,
I heaped up a tomb for Agamemnon, so that fame unquenchable might be his.
sentences.i: But when I had appeased the anger of the gods who are forever, I raised a tomb for Agamemnon, so that his fame might never go out.
sentences.n: κατέπαυσα, 'brought to a stop, checked', governs χόλον, 'anger', with the objective genitive θεῶν αἰὲν ἐόντων, the already-fixed 'the gods who are forever'. χεῦ(ε), aorist of χέω 'pour', is idiomatic of heaping up a burial mound. ἄσβεστον κλέος, 'fame unquenchable' (ἀ- + σβέννυμι 'quench'), plays on the image of a fire that will not go out; fixed here as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα τελευτήσας νεόμην, ἔδοσαν δέ μοι οὖρον
ἀθάνατοι, τοί μ’ ὦκα φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἔπεμψαν.
sentences.l:
Having brought these things to an end, I set out for home, and gave me a fair-wind
the immortals, who quickly to my dear fatherland sent me.
sentences.i: When I had finished all this, I set out for home, and the immortal gods gave me a fair wind and sent me quickly to my own dear fatherland.
sentences.n: τελευτήσας, aorist participle of τελευτάω 'bring to an end, complete'. νεόμην is imperfect of νέομαι 'return, go home' (cf. οἶκόνδε νέεσθαι, 1.17), with inceptive force, 'I set out for home'. οὖρον, 'a favouring wind', is the object of ἔδοσαν. φίλην... πατρίδα is the already-fixed formula, here first person.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἐπίμεινον ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἐμοῖσιν,
ὄφρα κεν ἑνδεκάτη τε δυωδεκάτη τε γένηται·
sentences.l:
But come now, stay on in my halls,
until the eleventh day and the twelfth shall come;
sentences.i: But come now, stay here in my halls, until the eleventh or twelfth day arrives;
sentences.n: This unit marks Menelaus's turn, within his still-open outer speech to Telemachus (opened at 4.333, not closed within this part), from narrating the past to addressing his young guest in the present; no new quotation mark is needed, since the frame has not changed speaker. ἑνδεκάτη...δυωδεκάτη (sc. ἡμέρᾳ), 'the eleventh...twelfth day', are ordinals used absolutely; Homeric hospitality commonly fixes a guest's stay to a round number of days before sending him off with gifts.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε σ’ εὖ πέμψω, δώσω δέ τοι ἀγλαὰ δῶρα,
τρεῖς ἵππους καὶ δίφρον ἐύξοον·
sentences.l:
and then well shall I send you off, and I shall give you splendid gifts,
three horses and a well-polished car;
sentences.i: and then I will send you off well provided, and give you splendid gifts — three horses and a well-polished chariot;
sentences.n: πέμψω...εὖ, 'send you well', implies sending a guest off properly equipped, the standard close of Homeric hospitality. ἀγλαὰ δῶρα pairs the already-fixed ἀγλαός 'splendid' with 'gifts'. δίφρον ἐύξοον, 'a well-polished car' (chariot-body), is a new noun-epithet pair fixed here — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
δώσω καλὸν ἄλεισον, ἵνα σπένδῃσθα θεοῖσιν
ἀθανάτοις ἐμέθεν μεμνημένος ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.l:
and then besides
I shall give you a fair goblet, so that you may pour libations to the gods,
the immortals, remembering me for all your days.”
sentences.i: and besides that I will give you a fine goblet, so that you may pour libations to the immortal gods and remember me all your days.”
sentences.n: ἄλεισον, 'goblet', is the already-fixed rendering reserved for this noun, distinct from the κρητήρ, 'mixing-bowl', named later in this part. μεμνημένος is the perfect participle of μιμνήσκομαι, with the genitive ἐμέθεν, 'of me'. ἤματα πάντα, 'for all your days', is a common closing tag, fixed here as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md. This unit's last words close Menelaus's very long outer speech to Telemachus, opened at 4.333, not touched again until the narrator resumes at 4.593.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This whole line is identical to 4.155 and to the house table's fixed fourth reply-formula, already published at odyssey-004 (ln 388); the same English is used again. Its appearance marks the narrator-level frame resuming after Menelaus's very long speech, itself just closed at the end of the previous unit.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη, μὴ δή με πολὺν χρόνον ἐνθάδ’ ἔρυκε.
sentences.l: “Son of Atreus, do not now for a long time here detain me.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, do not keep me here for long.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη, vocative, is the already-fixed periphrasis 'son of Atreus', here addressing Menelaus (contrast its use of Agamemnon elsewhere, e.g. 4.492). μή with the imperative ἔρυκε is a direct prohibition. This opens Telemachus's own speech, his first extended reply to Menelaus's hospitality, and takes a fresh top-level quotation mark, since the narrator's frame has just resumed at 4.593.

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ κ’ εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν ἐγὼ παρὰ σοί γ’ ἀνεχοίμην
ἥμενος, οὐδέ κέ μ’ οἴκου ἕλοι πόθος οὐδὲ τοκήων·
sentences.l:
For indeed for a year I could hold out, beside you,
sitting, nor would longing for home take hold of me, nor for my parents;
sentences.i: Indeed I could well hold out for a whole year sitting here beside you, with no longing for home or for my parents taking hold of me;
sentences.n: ἀνεχοίμην, potential optative with κε (= ἄν), 'I could bear to remain'. ἥμενος, present participle of ἧμαι 'sit', pictures him seated as an honoured guest. ἕλοι, aorist optative of αἱρέω, 'take hold of, seize', governs the genitives οἴκου and τοκήων, as a verb of longing often does.

sentences.t:
αἰνῶς γὰρ μύθοισιν ἔπεσσί τε σοῖσιν ἀκούων
τέρπομαι.
sentences.l:
for terribly, at your speeches and your words listening,
I take delight.
sentences.i: for I take wonderful delight in listening to your words and stories.
sentences.n: αἰνῶς, 'terribly, wondrously', intensifies pleasure here, not fear — the same adverb described the seals' smell at 4.441–442 (odyssey-018); context alone decides its force. μύθοισιν and ἔπεσσι, near-synonyms, are paired for emphasis. τέρπομαι, 'I take delight', is the same verb used of the suitors at their games later in this part (626).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤδη μοι ἀνιάζουσιν ἑταῖροι
ἐν Πύλῳ ἠγαθέῃ·
sentences.l:
But by now my companions are growing anxious for me
in holy Pylos;
sentences.i: but by now my companions must be growing anxious for me back in holy Pylos;
sentences.n: ἀνιάζουσιν, present of ἀνιάζω, 'be distressed, grow anxious' (the same verb used of Proteus's weariness at 4.460, odyssey-018), here of companions worrying over a long absence. Πύλῳ ἠγαθέῃ, 'holy Pylos' (ἠγαθέη, an intensive formation, literally 'very sacred'), is a distinct standing epithet from the already-fixed Πύλον ἠμαθόεντα 'sandy Pylos'; both are kept, and this one is fixed now as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t: σὺ δέ με χρόνον ἐνθάδ’ ἐρύκεις.
sentences.l: but you detain me here a long time.
sentences.i: and you are keeping me here so long.
sentences.n: ἐρύκεις, present of ἐρύκω 'hold back, detain', echoes ἔρυκε in Telemachus's own opening line (594); the repetition frames his whole speech.

sentences.t: δῶρον δ’ ὅττι κέ μοι δοίης, κειμήλιον ἔστω·
sentences.l: But whatever gift you might give me, let it be a keepsake;
sentences.i: Whatever gift you give me, let it be something to keep as a treasure;
sentences.n: ὅττι κε with the optative δοίης is an indefinite relative clause, 'whatever you might give'. κειμήλιον, 'a treasure laid up, a keepsake' (from κεῖμαι 'lie stored'), recurs of Menelaus's own treasures at 613 below; Telemachus asks for something to keep at home, not put to use on the road.

sentences.t:
ἵππους δ’ εἰς Ἰθάκην οὐκ ἄξομαι, ἀλλὰ σοὶ αὐτῷ
ἐνθάδε λείψω ἄγαλμα·
sentences.l:
But horses to Ithaca I will not lead away, but for you yourself
I will leave them here, a glory;
sentences.i: But I will not take horses to Ithaca; I will leave them here for you yourself, as an ornament for your own house;
sentences.n: ἄξομαι, future middle of ἄγω, 'I will lead away (for myself)'. ἄγαλμα, 'a glory, an ornament, a thing to delight in' (from ἀγάλλομαι 'take pride in'), is not the later sense 'statue'; Telemachus tactfully turns down the horses themselves, worth more as Menelaus's own showpiece than as cargo for rocky Ithaca.

sentences.t:
σὺ γὰρ πεδίοιο ἀνάσσεις
εὐρέος, ᾧ ἔνι μὲν λωτὸς πολύς, ἐν δὲ κύπειρον
πυροί τε ζειαί τε ἰδ’ εὐρυφυὲς κρῖ λευκόν.
sentences.i: for you rule a wide plain, where there is plenty of clover, and galingale, and wheat and spelt, and broad-eared white barley.
sentences.n: πεδίοιο... εὐρέος, 'a wide plain', describes the Eurotas valley around Sparta, suited to horse-pasture, in implied contrast with rocky Ithaca (605–608). λωτός here is read as a kind of clover or trefoil grazed by horses, the ordinary Homeric sense of the word in a pastoral catalogue like this one; this reading says nothing about how the word might be used in some other part of the poem. κύπειρον is 'galingale', a marsh sedge; ζειαί is 'spelt'; κρῖ, an old form of κριθή 'barley', is qualified by εὐρυφυές, 'broad-growing, spreading wide'.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ Ἰθάκῃ οὔτ’ ἂρ δρόμοι εὐρέες οὔτε τι λειμών·
sentences.l: but in Ithaca there are no wide race-courses, nor any meadow;
sentences.i: but in Ithaca there are no wide courses for horses, nor any meadow;
sentences.n: δρόμοι, 'race-courses, running-tracks', are what wide, level ground would be used for — horse- and chariot-exercise; their absence explains why horses would be wasted in Ithaca. λειμών, 'meadow, grassland', is likewise lacking; the two together are what a horse-country needs.

sentences.t: αἰγίβοτος, καὶ μᾶλλον ἐπήρατος ἱπποβότοιο.
sentences.l: goat-pastured, and more lovely than a horse-pastured land.
sentences.i: it is goat-pasturing land, and lovelier for that than one that pastures horses.
sentences.n: The subject, understood from Ἰθάκη in the line before, is left unexpressed: '[Ithaca is] goat-pastured'. αἰγίβοτος and ἱπποβότοιο, 'goat-pastured' and 'of a horse-pastured (land)', are formed alike from βόσκω 'graze'; ἐπήρατος, 'lovely, desired', takes the genitive of comparison. Telemachus turns what might sound like a deficiency into a matter of pride.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τις νήσων ἱππήλατος οὐδ’ ἐυλείμων,
αἵ θ’ ἁλὶ κεκλίαται·
sentences.l:
For no one of the islands is fit for driving horses, nor rich in meadow,
of those that lie upon the sea;
sentences.i: For none of the islands that lie out on the sea is fit for driving horses or rich in meadow;
sentences.n: ἱππήλατος, 'fit for driving horses upon', and ἐυλείμων, 'rich in meadow', are both negated together. κεκλίαται, perfect passive-in-form of κλίνω 'lean, lie', with Ionic -αται for -νται (cf. δεδαίαται, 1.23), describes the islands as 'lying' upon the sea; the epic τε marks a general truth.

sentences.t: Ἰθάκη δέ τε καὶ περὶ πασέων.
sentences.l: but Ithaca is beyond all of them.”
sentences.i: but Ithaca surpasses them all.”
sentences.n: περὶ with the genitive πασέων ('of all') is used adverbially, 'above, beyond', with an understood verb of excelling; the epic τε again marks a standing truth. This closes Telemachus's speech, the first extended one he has spoken since arriving in Sparta.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος,
χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and smiled, good-at-the-war-cry Menelaus,
and stroked him with his hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Menelaus, good at the war-cry, smiled, and stroked him with his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the fixed formula 'so he spoke'. βοὴν ἀγαθός is the already-fixed epithet of Menelaus. κατέρεξεν, aorist of καταρρέζω 'stroke, caress', is a gentler gesture than the hand-clasp of the already-fixed two-line approach formula; its tail, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε(ν), repeats that formula's own closing words, and the same English is kept for it. This whole gesture-and-address formula is new and is fixed as such — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t: αἵματός εἰς ἀγαθοῖο, φίλον τέκος, οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις·
sentences.l: “Of good blood you are, dear child, such things you say;
sentences.i: “You are of good blood, dear child, to judge by what you say;
sentences.n: αἵματός... ἀγαθοῖο, 'of good blood', a partitive genitive of origin with εἰς ('you are'), praises Telemachus's breeding as shown by his speech. φίλον τέκος, 'dear child', is a fresh vocative of endearment, distinct from the already-fixed τέκνον ἐμόν; οἷα, neuter plural, is exclamatory, 'what things you say!'.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι ταῦτα μεταστήσω·
sentences.l: Therefore I will change these things for you;
sentences.i: So then, I will change these gifts for you;
sentences.n: τοιγάρ, 'therefore, accordingly', introduces a consequence drawn from what has just been praised. μεταστήσω, future of μεθίστημι, 'change, alter, substitute', announces that Menelaus will swap the horses and chariot for something else, as Telemachus has just asked.

sentences.t: δύναμαι γάρ.
sentences.l: for I am able.
sentences.i: for I have the means to do it.
sentences.n: δύναμαι, 'I am able, I have the power/means', is a plain closing justification: Menelaus's wealth makes the substitution an easy matter for him.

sentences.t:
δώρων δ’ ὅσσ’ ἐν ἐμῷ οἴκῳ κειμήλια κεῖται,
δώσω ὃ κάλλιστον καὶ τιμηέστατόν ἐστιν·
sentences.l:
But of the gifts, as many treasures as in my house lie stored,
I will give the one that is fairest and most honoured;
sentences.i: Of all the treasures stored up as gifts in my house, I will give you the one that is finest and most highly prized;
sentences.n: κειμήλια, 'treasures laid up', repeats the noun Telemachus himself used at 600. κεῖται, present of κεῖμαι, matches the verb's root sense, 'lie stored'. τιμηέστατον, superlative of τιμήεις, 'held in honour, precious', pairs with κάλλιστον, 'fairest', to describe the single choicest object among all his stored gifts.

sentences.t: δώσω τοι κρητῆρα τετυγμένον·
sentences.l: I will give you a wrought mixing-bowl;
sentences.i: I will give you a well-wrought mixing-bowl;
sentences.n: κρητήρ is the large bowl in which wine was mixed with water before serving, a common prestige gift. τετυγμένον, perfect passive participle of τεύχω 'make, fashion', 'wrought, well-made', is a standing mark of fine craftsmanship likely to recur with other objects; fixed here as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
ἀργύρεος δὲ
ἔστιν ἅπας, χρυσῷ δ’ ἐπὶ χείλεα κεκράανται,
ἔργον δ’ Ἡφαίστοιο.
sentences.l:
silver
it is entirely, and with gold upon its rims it has been finished,
the work of Hephaestus.
sentences.i: it is entirely silver, its rims finished with gold, the work of Hephaestus.
sentences.n: ἀργύρεος, 'silver, made of silver', is a material adjective. κεκράανται, perfect passive of κραίνω 'accomplish, finish off', describes metalwork finishing the rims (χείλεα) with an overlay of gold. ἔργον Ἡφαίστοιο, 'the work of Hephaestus', is the standing Homeric mark of the finest divine craftsmanship, fixed here as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
πόρεν δέ ἑ Φαίδιμος ἥρως,
Σιδονίων βασιλεύς, ὅθ’ ἑὸς δόμος ἀμφεκάλυψε
κεῖσέ με νοστήσαντα·
sentences.i: Phaedimus the hero, king of the Sidonians, gave it to me, when his own house sheltered me there on my journey home;
sentences.n: πόρεν, aorist of the defective verb πόρω, 'gave, granted'. ἥρως, 'the hero', is the already-fixed plain title. Σιδονίων βασιλεύς places the gift's origin in Phoenician Sidon, a byword in Homer for fine metalwork; ἀμφεκάλυψε, 'enclosed, sheltered' (ἀμφί + καλύπτω), pictures the house wrapping around its guest; νοστήσαντα agrees with the unexpressed 'me', on some earlier voyage of Menelaus's own not otherwise detailed here.

sentences.t: τεῒν δ’ ἐθέλω τόδ’ ὀπάσσαι.
sentences.l: and to you I wish to give this.”
sentences.i: and now I want to give it to you.”
sentences.n: τεΐν is an epic dative of σύ, 'to you' (= Attic σοί). ὀπάσσαι, aorist infinitive of ὀπάζω, 'to grant, bestow', with ἐθέλω. This closes Menelaus's reply and the whole conversation of the Sparta scene, which the next unit summarises from outside.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
δαιτυμόνες δ’ ἐς δώματ’ ἴσαν θείου βασιλῆος.
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
and the feasters went to the halls of the godlike king.
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, and the guests went in to the halls of the godlike king.
sentences.n: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον is a narrator's summary line closing the whole dialogue, distinct from a speech-closing formula: it reports that conversation continued, not any single speech's end, and needs no quotation mark. δαιτυμόνες, 'those at the feast, guests'; θείου βασιλῆος, 'the godlike king', is Menelaus himself, seen now from outside as other guests arrive.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἦγον μὲν μῆλα, φέρον δ’ ἐυήνορα οἶνον·
sentences.l: and they led sheep, and carried strengthening wine;
sentences.i: Some led in sheep, and others brought wine to hearten the men;
sentences.n: ἦγον and φέρον, both imperfects, describe the guests' customary contributions to a feast: driving in animals for sacrifice, and bringing wine. ἐυήνορα, 'making men brave' (ἐύ + ἀνήρ), is a standing epithet of wine, translated by its sense rather than literally, since 'well-manly wine' would mislead.

sentences.t: σῖτον δέ σφ’ ἄλοχοι καλλικρήδεμνοι ἔπεμπον.
sentences.l: and bread for them their fair-veiled wives were sending.
sentences.i: and their fair-veiled wives sent bread for them.
sentences.n: σῖτος, 'grain, bread', is the staple food-word paired with wine throughout Homer. καλλικρήδεμνοι, 'fair-veiled' (κρήδεμνον, a woman's veil or headband), describes the guests' own wives sending provisions from their separate homes for the shared feast.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν περὶ δεῖπνον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι πένοντο.
sentences.l: So they were busied about the meal in the halls.
sentences.i: So they busied themselves with the meal in the halls.
sentences.n: πένοντο, imperfect middle of πένομαι, 'toil at, be busy with', with περὶ δεῖπνον, 'about the meal'. This closing line ends the Sparta scene before the narrative shifts to Ithaca in the next unit, within the same Murray paragraph.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρες δὲ πάροιθεν Ὀδυσσῆος μεγάροιο
δίσκοισιν τέρποντο καὶ αἰγανέῃσιν ἱέντες
ἐν τυκτῷ δαπέδῳ, ὅθι περ πάρος, ὕβριν ἔχοντες.
sentences.l:
But the suitors, in front of the hall of Odysseus,
with discuses were taking delight, and with javelins throwing,
on the smoothed pavement, where indeed before, holding their insolence.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the suitors, in front of Odysseus's hall, were amusing themselves throwing the discus and the javelin on the levelled floor, where they always did, indulging their insolence as before.
sentences.n: τέρποντο, imperfect middle, matches τέρπομαι at 598, but now of games rather than of speech. αἰγανέῃσιν, 'light javelins, hunting-spears', distinct from the heavier δόρυ of battle; ἱέντες, present participle of ἵημι 'throw, hurl'. τυκτῷ δαπέδῳ, 'the wrought, levelled floor', names a prepared open courtyard used for games. ὕβριν ἔχοντες, 'holding insolence', names the suitors' whole way of life at Odysseus's expense, not this game alone.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνοος δὲ καθῆστο καὶ Εὐρύμαχος θεοειδής,
ἀρχοὶ μνηστήρων, ἀρετῇ δ’ ἔσαν ἔξοχ’ ἄριστοι.
sentences.l:
And Antinous was sitting, and Eurymachus, godlike-in-form,
the leaders of the suitors, and in excellence they were far the best.
sentences.i: Antinous was sitting there, and Eurymachus, godlike in form, the leaders of the suitors, who were far the best of them in excellence.
sentences.n: καθῆστο, pluperfect-in-form of κάθημαι, with imperfect sense, 'was sitting', apart from the others' games. θεοειδής is the already-fixed 'godlike in form'. ἀρχοί, 'leaders, chiefs', names Antinous and Eurymachus as the suitors' two ringleaders throughout the poem. ἀρετῇ, dative of respect, 'in excellence'; ἔξοχ(α), adverbial, 'exceedingly'.

sentences.t:
τοῖς δ’ υἱὸς Φρονίοιο Νοήμων ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
Ἀντίνοον μύθοισιν ἀνειρόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.l:
And to them the son of Phronius, Noemon, coming near,
Antinous with words, asking, addressed:
sentences.i: Then Noemon, son of Phronius, came up to them and put a question to Antinous:
sentences.n: Νοήμων, 'Noemon', son of Φρόνιος (a speaking name, 'the thoughtful one'), is a minor Ithacan who earlier lent Telemachus his ship for the voyage to Pylos, not itself narrated in this part. ἀνειρόμενος, present participle of ἀνείρομαι, 'ask, inquire', governs μύθοισιν, 'with words'. προσέειπεν closes the introductory formula; the question itself opens the next unit.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνο’, ἦ ῥά τι ἴδμεν ἐνὶ φρεσίν, ἦε καὶ οὐκί,
ὁππότε Τηλέμαχος νεῖτ’ ἐκ Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος;
sentences.l:
“Antinous, do we indeed know at all in our minds, or not,
when Telemachus is to return from sandy Pylos?
sentences.i: “Antinous, do any of us happen to know, or not, when Telemachus is coming back from sandy Pylos?
sentences.n: ἴδμεν, 'we know' (perfect with present sense, = Attic ἴσμεν), with ἐνὶ φρεσίν, 'in our minds', is a formula of inquiry; ἦε καὶ οὐκί, 'or not', is a standard alternative-question tag. νεῖται, present with future sense, 'is returning'. Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος is the already-fixed 'sandy Pylos', genitive. This opens Noemon's speech, a fresh top-level quotation, since the narrator's frame closed at 631.

sentences.t: νῆά μοι οἴχετ’ ἄγων·
sentences.l: My ship he has gone off, leading it away;
sentences.i: He has gone off with my ship;
sentences.n: οἴχεται, present with perfect sense, 'is gone, has gone off' (a verb regularly used this way in Homer), with the participle ἄγων, 'leading, taking'; νῆα, though placed before both verbs, is grammatically the object of ἄγων alone, since οἴχεται itself is intransitive. Noemon reveals only now, almost in passing, that it was his own ship Telemachus took.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δὲ χρεὼ γίγνεται αὐτῆς
Ἤλιδ’ ἐς εὐρύχορον διαβήμεναι, ἔνθα μοι ἵπποι
δώδεκα θήλειαι, ὑπὸ δ’ ἡμίονοι ταλαεργοὶ
ἀδμῆτες·
sentences.l:
and for me there arises need of it,
to Elis of-wide-dancing-grounds to cross over, where I have mares
twelve, and under them mules, labour-enduring,
unbroken;
sentences.i: and now I have need of it myself, to cross over to spacious Elis, where I have twelve mares, and under them mules bred of them, labour-enduring and still unbroken;
sentences.n: χρεὼ γίγνεται, 'a need arises', is an impersonal idiom with the genitive αὐτῆς, 'of it (the ship)'. εὐρύχορον, 'of wide dancing-places, spacious', a standing place-epithet, is fixed here as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md. ὑπὸ... ἡμίονοι, 'mules under them', uses ὑπό in the sense 'begotten under, born of': mules are the offspring of mares by a donkey-sire, so 'under' marks the mares as their dams. ταλαεργοί, 'enduring toil', a standing epithet of mules, is fixed as a new rendering — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t: τῶν κέν τιν’ ἐλασσάμενος δαμασαίμην.
sentences.l: one of which, driving it off, I might break in.”
sentences.i: and I want to drive one of them off and break it in myself.”
sentences.n: τῶν is partitive, 'of them'; ἐλασσάμενος, aorist middle participle of ἐλαύνω, 'drive off (for oneself)'; δαμασαίμην, aorist optative middle of δαμάζω, 'tame, break in', with κε for potential force. This closes Noemon's speech and his whole part in the poem's action here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ἐθάμβεον·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they in their spirit were amazed;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they were astonished in their hearts;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ(ο) is the fixed closing formula. ἀνὰ θυμὸν ἐθάμβεον, 'were amazed up and down their spirit' (ἀνά used distributively), θαμβέω 'be astonished, marvel'; the imperfect describes their reaction as it set in. This is plain narration; the suitors' amazement, not yet explained, is unpacked in the unit that follows.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔφαντο
ἐς Πύλον οἴχεσθαι Νηλήιον, ἀλλά που αὐτοῦ
ἀγρῶν ἢ μήλοισι παρέμμεναι ἠὲ συβώτῃ.
sentences.l:
for they did not suppose
to Neleian Pylos he had gone, but that somewhere there
among the fields, or with the flocks, he was staying, or with the swineherd.
sentences.i: for they had not supposed that he had gone off to Neleian Pylos, but that he was staying somewhere close by, among the fields or the flocks, or with the swineherd.
sentences.n: ἔφαντο, imperfect middle of φημί, 'they supposed, believed'. Νηλήιον, 'Neleian', names Pylos for its founder-king Neleus, Nestor's father, distinct from the already-fixed ἠμαθόεις 'sandy' and ἠγαθέη 'holy'. παρέμμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι of πάρειμι, 'to be near, be present'; συβώτῃ, 'with the swineherd', names Eumaeus's office without yet naming the man, whom the poem has not yet introduced. This closing unit ends the part with the suitors still unaware that Telemachus's absence is a real journey.
